articles.title: Shared Fine-Scale Functional Organization in the Human Subcortex Revealed by Connectivity Hyperalignment
articles.content: Subcortical structures are central to cognition, emotion, and social processing, and their dysfunction underlies a wide range of neurological and psychiatric conditions. Yet subcortical fine-scale functional organization has remained largely inaccessible to group-level fMRI analysis: nuclei are small and low-SNR, and their functional topography varies idiosyncratically across individuals in ways that anatomical alignment cannot resolve. This idiosyncrasy carries real stakes. For example, deep brain stimulation targets with more variable functional connectivity across individuals show correspondingly less consistent clinical outcomes. Here we show that this seemingly idiosyncratic subcortical organization in fact reflects shared, fine-grained structure that can be recovered by modeling each individual's connectivity in a common functional space (connectivity hyperalignment, CHA), rather than relying on anatomical correspondence. Applying CHA to fMRI data collected during naturalistic movie viewing, we found that aligning subcortical voxels by their cortical connectivity, rather than their anatomical location, sharply increased cross-subject correspondence in both stimulus-evoked response and connectivity profiles. Critically, this alignment sharpened rather than blurred local structure: neighboring voxels became more functionally distinct from one another, and cortical connectivity targets became substantially more decodable across subjects. These results indicate that human subcortical nuclei possess a common fine-scale functional architecture that is masked by anatomical variability but recoverable at the individual level. This reframes a central methodological constraint in subcortical neuroimaging: rather than trading spatial resolution for signal quality via smoothing, group-level analyses can achieve voxel-level precision by aligning function rather than anatomy, opening a path to studying cortical-subcortical circuit organization in greater detail.
articles.author: Tu, J. C., Feilong, M., Zhang, Y., Gobbini, M. I., Haxby, J. V.

articles.title: Synaptic density imaging associates with performance but not self-report in autism
articles.content: Autism is a common neurodevelopmental condition with considerable between-person variability and unknown biological etiology. Diagnosis of autism in adults relies on measurement of performance (e.g., clinician rating of social behavior, standardized assessment of cognition) and self-report of autism features. Our prior work revealed a strong relationship between clinician ratings of social function in autism and in vivo measures of synaptic density as measured by [11C]UCB-J PET (Matuskey et al., 2025). However, it is not understood how the measured aspects of the autism phenotype index underlying biology. Here, in a sample of 12 autistic adults, we address this question by relating synaptic density imaging to a range of performance measures, such as cognition and face recognition, in contrast to self-report measures. Our results identify a dissociation between these measurement types in that synaptic density correlates strongly with measures of performance but shows virtually no relationship with self-report. These findings suggest that, while self-report and performance measures share variance in characterizing phenotypes in autism, they diverge when mapping onto the underlying biology. Results suggest that higher synaptic density may index a general mechanism that facilitates social and cognitive performance across a range of tasks. These data also indicate that performance and self-report measures are not interchangeable in capturing brain-behavior correspondences in autism, a finding that can guide measure selection in future biomarker studies and clinical research.
articles.author: Naples, A. J., Cayir, S., cukar-capizzi, C., Wolf, J. M., Mcclelland, J. E., Robertson, E. C., Sawant, S. S., Matuskey, D., McPartland, J.

articles.title: Thalamic Dysconnectivity and Negative Symptoms in Schizophrenia Spectrum Disorder
articles.content: Background and Hypothesis Negative symptoms in schizophrenia spectrum disorder (SSD) are associated with poor functional outcomes and reduced quality of life; however, effective treatments remain limited. A better understanding of the underlying brain mechanisms is needed to develop better treatments. Neuroimaging studies implicate multiple brain networks in negative symptoms, though findings remain heterogeneous, potentially reflecting the multidimensionality of both symptoms and brain networks. Larger, more systematic dissections are required to identify the key hub(s) underlying negative symptoms. Study Design Structural MRI data from 394 participants (210 SSD, 184 healthy controls [HC]) were analyzed to identify cortical thickness and subcortical volume demonstrating both SSD-HC differences and associations with negative symptoms measured by the Brief Negative Symptom Scale (BNSS). Regions meeting both criteria were selected as seeds for resting-state functional connectivity analyses in 143 SSD patients to examine association with negative symptoms and their subdomains. Study Results The thalamus was the only region demonstrating significant structural abnormalities both in SSD and an association with BNSS total score (p-FDR<0.05). Functional-network-defined thalamic subregions were subsequently examined. Several thalamic hypoconnectivities were significantly corresponded with negative symptoms, involving thalamic subregions associated with the cortical default mode, somatosensory, medial temporal, and dorsal attention networks (p=0.001, corrected<0.05). Blunted affect showed the most extensive thalamic connectivity alterations, involving the striatum, cerebellum, and temporoparietal junction/superior temporal sulcus (TPJ-STS). Thalamic hypoconnectivity with TPJ-STS was also associated with overall negative symptoms and anhedonia. Conclusions This study identifies the thalamus as a central hub of negative symptom-related dysfunction in SSD and highlights specific thalamic subnetworks as potential targets for circuit-based interventions.
articles.author: Kunitoki, K., Adhikari, B. M., Ankeeta, A., Gao, S., Ma, Y., Straub, K. T., Dos Santos Alves Maria, G., Pagan, A. F., Warner, A. R., Du, X., Kochunov, P., Hong, L. E.

articles.title: Clustered and diffuse sensory corticostriatal wirings define complementary interneuron circuits
articles.content: In the striatum, interneurons tightly control the activity of output neurons, the striatal projection neurons (SPN). Among these striatal interneurons, parvalbumin-expressing (PV) and somatostatin-expressing (SOM) cells exhibit markedly distinct electrophysiological and anatomical properties, suggesting differential integration into striatal circuits and distinct forms of feedforward inhibition onto SPN. However, it remains unclear whether differences already emerge at the level of corticostriatal connectivity and if they shape specific interactions with cortical inputs to SPN. Here, we investigated the spatial organization of the projections from the primary and secondary somatosensory areas (S1 and S2), onto striatal PV and SOM interneurons and SPN. With a combination of anatomical tracing and functional circuit mapping, we characterized key features of corticostriatal connectivity, including input number, origin, spacing, overlap and strength. We found that input spacing and strength, at both the individual cell and population levels, were the principal features distinguishing PV and SOM interneurons. In contrast, connectivity differed primarily in input number and laminar organization across S1 and S2. Our findings suggest two potential modes of interaction between interneurons and SPN connectivity: one in which PV interneurons receive S1 inputs structured in large clusters, that densely overlap with those of neighboring SPN, providing an anatomical substrate for potential neuronal assemblies. And another in which SOM interneurons also receive abundant cortical inputs, but thinly disseminated across S1 and S2 and that overlap little with those of SPN, potentially shaping these cell integration through input cross-interaction. These cell-type principles of corticostriatal wiring may support distinct forms of striatal computation.

Approximate matrix exponential: a fast and accurate solver for Markov kinetic models of ion channels
articles.content: A new method is presented for simulating Markov kinetic models of ion channels, which are biologically realistic but difficult to simulate. Computing the analytic solution is prohibitively expensive, necessitating the use of numerical methods. The new method creates a piecewise polynomial approximation of the propagator matrix, which is the analytic solution operator. The new method is an order of magnitude faster and more accurate than previous numerical methods, but it is limited to models with one or two input variables and its time complexity scales quadratically with the number of model states. The accompanying program, ame, applies the new method to the NEURON simulator. For comparison, the analytic solution was also added to NEURON. The new method achieves real-time performance on a state-of-the-art GPU for tens to hundreds of thousands of model instances. This method will allow large-scale neuronal simulations to use more detailed models of ion channels.
articles.author: David Alton McDougall

articles.title: An attention-enhanced hybrid CNN-BiLSTM framework for multiclass epileptic seizure recognition using EEG signals
articles.content: IntroductionElectroencephalogram (EEG) signal classification plays a pivotal role in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) and the diagnosis of neurological disorders. However, the non-stationary, non-linear, and low signal-to-noise ratio characteristics of EEG signals make accurate feature extraction challenging. Conventional deep learning approaches often struggle to simultaneously capture localized transient patterns, deep temporal dependencies, and long-range contextual relationships within EEG signals.MethodsTo address these challenges, an optimized end-to-end hybrid deep learning framework, termed CNN–BiLSTM–MHSA, is proposed for multiclass epileptic seizure recognition. The architecture sequentially integrates a multilayer one-dimensional Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for localized feature extraction, a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network for capturing forward and backward temporal dependencies, and a Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA) mechanism for dynamically emphasizing discriminative neurological events. Robust preprocessing includes Butterworth bandpass filtering, Z-score normalization, and data augmentation using Gaussian noise injection and amplitude scaling. The framework was evaluated on the UCI/Kaggle Epileptic Seizure Recognition dataset comprising 11,500 EEG segments distributed across five classes.ResultsThe proposed framework achieved an overall accuracy of 98.83%, precision of 98.95%, recall (sensitivity) of 98.84%, F1-score of 98.90%, specificity of 99.71%, balanced accuracy of 98.84%, ROC-AUC of 99.80%, and PR-AUC of 99.72%. Class-wise accuracies exceeded 99% for most categories, with one seizure class achieving perfect recognition. Comparative evaluation further demonstrated that the proposed framework outperformed several recent state-of-the-art EEG seizure classification methods.DiscussionThe superior performance can be attributed to the complementary representation capabilities of the hybrid architecture. CNN layers effectively learn localized signal patterns, BiLSTM captures bidirectional temporal dependencies, and MHSA enhances the representation of long-range contextual relationships by assigning greater importance to informative temporal regions. The combination of robust preprocessing and data augmentation further contributes to improved generalization and classification reliability.
articles.author: Ahmed H. Almutairi

articles.title: Validating electrical stimulation through the somatosensory system: a perspective on mismatch negativity and auditory prostheses
articles.content: Natural touch engages specialized mechanoreceptors, while electrotactile stimulation bypasses them, directly depolarizing a mixed and non-uniform population of afferent axons. Whether this difference in peripheral encoding affects the brain predictive processing remains an open empirical question. The mismatch negativity (MMN), an established electroencephalography (EEG) marker of automatic change detection, provides a powerful tool to address this question without perceptual confounds. Somatosensory studies comparing MMN responses to natural versus electrical stimulation within the same healthy individuals can identify candidate mechanisms for testing in the auditory domain, where such designs are inherently not feasible. In particular, they can help disentangle device effects from deafness-related confounds in cochlear implant (CI) users. Existing somatosensory evidence in healthy subjects suggests that electrotactile stimulation elicits mismatch responses with less bilateral integration than natural touch, though this evidence remains limited to a single magnetoencephalography (MEG) study using an oddball paradigm. CI studies are more extensive and show feature-specific MMN deficits. However, they also rely on oddball or multi-feature paradigms that conflate prediction error with sensory adaptation. This Perspective therefore encourages the adoption of alternative MMN paradigms (roving, omission, or local–global) to determine whether electrical stimulation truly engages the brain’s predictive machinery. With emerging multimodal stimulators, the somatosensory system offers a valuable platform to test whether electrical stimulation reproduces natural predictive processing—insights that can improve both tactile neuroprostheses and CI devices.
articles.author: Boriss Sagalajev

articles.title: Behavioural expression of ictal embarrassment: a stereo-EEG case report
articles.content: Embarrassment is a rare ictal manifestation whose neurophysiological basis remains poorly understood. We describe the case of a 40-year-old woman with drug-resistant focal epilepsy characterized by an unusual ictal semiology combining an intense positive emotional experience with behavioral manifestations of embarrassment. Stereo-EEG demonstrated seizure onset within the middle frontal gyrus bank of the superior frontal sulcus (F2sb), with rapid propagation to the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC) and superior anterior insula (sAI). Electrical stimulation of the F2sb reliably reproduced the habitual electroclinical seizure. While identical stimulation parameters elicited the subjective and autonomic manifestations in both supine and upright postures, the complete behavioral repertoire of embarrassment emerged only when stimulation was delivered in the standing position. Exploratory functional connectivity analyses revealed that overt embarrassment was associated with reduced node strength within a network encompassing the dACC, sAI, mesial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC). More restricted network changes were associated with only mild sensations, whereas asymptomatic stimulation produced a distinct and partly reversed connectivity pattern. This case suggests that the behavioral expression of ictal embarrassment arises from the transient reconfiguration of a frontal-cingulo-insular network and is critically shaped by bodily context.
articles.author: L. Tassi

articles.title: Morphology beyond the morpheme: distributed processing effects in the acoustic realization of German word-final clusters
articles.content: This study investigates how morphological structure shapes phonetic realization in German word-final /Cst/ clusters, with a focus on form-meaning mapping strategies in elicited speech. Phonologically identical clusters are compared across simplex words and inflected verb forms, where /st/ encodes a grammatical morpheme. We analyse duration, intensity, and spectral center of gravity (COG) for clusters, individual segments, and adjacent vowels, modeling their variation with linear mixed-effects models. Rather than yielding uniform phonetic shifts, morphology-related effects emerge as context-sensitive patterns modulated by lexical and phonetic factors. Temporal effects primarily take the form of durational reduction in of morphemic segments, but they extend to surrounding phonetic material, where they manifest as lengthening. In addition, increased intensity and spectral sharpening are associated with morphemic shortening, calling for a more comprehensive interpretation of phonetic reduction and its relationship with morphological function. Overall, the results are in line with approaches to speech production that move beyond a strictly modular view and posit dynamic interactions between morphological and phonetic information within the cognitive system.
articles.author: Martina Rossi

articles.title: Anticipating interactions: a predictive diffusion framework for evolving bimanual manipulation
articles.content: IntroductionBimanual robotic manipulation remains a significant challenge in embodied AI, as it requires synchronized motion planning, inter-arm collision avoidance, and dynamic role allocation over long task horizons. Although existing diffusion-based policies and affordance learning methods have demonstrated considerable capability, they largely treat the environment as static and fail to model how interaction relationships and coordination patterns evolve over time.MethodsThis paper introduces the Predictive Affordance and Coordination Evolution Diffusion Policy (PACE-DP), a unified framework that explicitly forecasts future scene dynamics and models the temporal progression of manipulation affordances and bimanual coordination. PACE-DP integrates three predictive components: (1) a Predictive Scene Module that forecasts latent future object-centric representations; (2) an Affordance and Coordination Evolution Module that constructs temporally evolving interaction graphs and employs a Graph Transformer to predict future relation types, grasp success probabilities, coordination modes, and spatial alignment targets; and (3) a Conditional Diffusion Policy that generates smooth, coordinated action sequences conditioned on fused current and predicted features.ResultsWe evaluate PACE-DP on the RoboTwin 2.0 platform across 10 diverse bimanual tasks, including handover, placement, stacking, and switch operation. Experimental results show that PACE-DP performs favorably compared with baseline methods, achieving higher success rates on coordination-intensive tasks with only marginal computational overhead.DiscussionThese findings suggest that explicitly predicting future affordance and coordination evolution provides an effective inductive bias for bimanual manipulation, enabling more reliable coordination without substantially increasing computational cost. PACE-DP thus offers a promising step toward predictive, temporally aware policies for long-horizon bimanual tasks.
articles.author: Shenggang Wei

articles.title: Transspinal temporal interference stimulation enhances neuroplasticity-associated responses and facilitates motor recovery after spinal cord injury in mice
articles.content: IntroductionSpinal cord injury (SCI) causes substantial motor impairment, driven by neuronal loss, axonal disruption, and impaired synaptic connectivity. Temporal interference (TI) stimulation is capable of modulating neural activity, but its therapeutic potential in SCI remains largely unexplored. We explored the influence of TI stimulation on functional recovery and neuroplasticity-associated responses following SCI.MethodsThirty-two C57BL/6J mice were randomly allocated to four groups: sham, SCI, sham stimulation, and TI stimulation. Mice underwent T8 spinal cord hemisection, followed by daily TI stimulation from day 4 to day 21 post-injury. Locomotor recovery was evaluated using the Basso Mouse Scale (BMS). At 21 days after injury, neuronal-associated changes, glial responses, and neuroplasticity-associated molecular changes were assessed by immunofluorescence staining and western blot analysis.ResultsCompared with sham-operated mice, SCI mice exhibited impaired locomotor function, reduced NeuN-positive neuronal density, and decreased expression of neuroplasticity-associated proteins, including GAP43, NF-L, SYN, and PSD95. In contrast, TI stimulation significantly improved BMS scores and increased NeuN-positive neuronal density, accompanied by enhanced expression of axonal growth-associated proteins (GAP43 and NF-L) and synaptic plasticity-associated markers (SYN and PSD95).DiscussionThese findings indicate that TI stimulation improves functional recovery after SCI and is associated with enhanced neuroplasticity-related responses, including axonal growth-associated and synaptic plasticity-associated changes. This study provides evidence supporting TI stimulation as a promising neuromodulation strategy for promoting neuroplasticity-associated recovery processes after spinal cord injury.
articles.author: Shuang Wu

articles.title: MSANet: a multi-scale spatiotemporal adaptive network for EEG-based driver fatigue recognition
articles.content: Electroencephalography (EEG)-based driver fatigue recognition remains challenging because fatigue-related patterns are distributed across multiple temporal scales, inter-channel relationships vary across samples, and inter-individual differences complicate cross-subject transfer. To address these issues, a multi-scale spatiotemporal adaptive network (MSANet) is proposed for EEG-based driver fatigue recognition. The framework introduces a multi-granularity patch temporal gate (MGPTG) to model locally continuous temporal contexts, stable graph node enhancement (SGNE) to enhance channel-node features before dynamic graph construction, and an adaptive classifier gate (ACG) to combine cosine-based and affine decision geometries. MSANet was evaluated on two public simulated-driving EEG datasets using a cross-subject transfer protocol, in which the target-subject samples were stratified with a partition ratio of 0.5 into a labeled adaptation subset and a held-out test subset. MSANet achieved an accuracy (ACC) of 83.64% and an F1-score (F1) of 83.74% on Dataset I, and 74.64% ACC and 72.92% F1 on Dataset II. The results indicate strong numerical performance on Dataset I and competitive performance on Dataset II. Subject-level statistical analysis was additionally conducted to distinguish mean performance differences from differences that are consistently supported across subjects. Ablation results showed lower mean performance after removing MGPTG, SGNE, or ACG under the evaluated settings. These findings support further evaluation of the proposed stage-specific temporal, graph-node, and classification mechanisms for cross-subject transfer in EEG-based driver fatigue recognition.
articles.author: Xiaosong Peng

articles.title: Mixed emotions evoked when incongruent outward appearance and motion are combined
articles.content: Understanding mixed emotions is crucial for capturing the ambivalence of human information processing. However, how specific visual factors, such as outward appearance and motion, interact to evoke these conflicting feelings remains unclear. Here, we present three-dimensional (3D) characters as visual stimuli that evoke mixed feelings, providing empirical insights into emotional phenomena such as “kimo-kawaii” by focusing on their outward appearances and motions. Congruent stimuli (e.g., pleasant appearance with pleasant motion) and incongruent stimuli (e.g., pleasant appearance with unpleasant motion) were evaluated. Characters with congruent features evoked a single feeling: pleasant or unpleasant. In contrast, the combination of pleasant outward appearance and unpleasant motion evoked both pleasant and unpleasant feelings. Moreover, the combination of unpleasant outward appearance and pleasant motion strongly evoked unpleasant feelings rather than pleasant feelings. These findings suggest that, within the present stimulus set, outward appearance may exert a stronger influence on affective evaluation than motion. The observed co-activation of positive and negative affect may be relevant to mixed affective experiences such as “kimo-kawaii,” although further research using construct-specific measures is needed to establish this relationship.
articles.author: Hiroshi Yamada

articles.title: Subject-independent classification of ADHD from pediatric EEG: a leakage-aware deep learning framework with interpretable neurophysiological mapping
articles.content: BackgroundThe use of electroencephalography (EEG) in automated screening of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) has created a large body of literature that suggests promising outcomes, with reported classification accuracies often above 90%. A major methodological issue suggests that a substantial part of these results are actually due to data leakage, whereby EEG epochs pertaining to the same subject end up in both training and testing sets, allowing classifiers to capitalize on features specific to the individual rather than on genuine disorder-related biomarkers.MethodsWe assessed the performance of three classical machine learning algorithms, namely, Logistic Regression (LR), Random Forest (RF), and Support Vector Machine (SVM), as well as three deep learning models: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), and CNN-BiLSTM, on a standard pediatric EEG dataset containing 121 children and 4,173 epochs. The performance of each model was compared in terms of both segment-wise cross-validation (Protocol A) and subject-wise cross-validation (without any data leakage, Protocol B).To evaluate neurotopographic plausibility without making unsupported causal assertions, we applied Deep SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to the best-generalizing architecture.ResultsThe performance discrepancy was substantial. Under segment-wise evaluation, the SVM operating on power spectral density (PSD) features reached 90.0% accuracy (95% CI: [89.1%, 90.9%], AUC = 0.96). However, the same model dropped to 65.6% (95% CI: [62.1%, 69.1%], AUC = 0.72) under subject-wise evaluation—a statistically significant 24.4 percentage point collapse (p < 0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank). In contrast, deep architectures learning directly from raw EEG were resilient: the stand-alone CNN lost only 2.5 percentage points, achieving 72.7% accuracy (95% CI: [66.0%, 79.4%], AUC = 0.72, recall = 88.0%) on completely unseen participants. Post-hoc SHAP attribution identified the highest relative contributions in frontal (F3, Fz, F4) and central (Cz) electrodes, aligning with established ADHD neurophysiology.ConclusionHand-engineered spectral features are highly vulnerable to identity leakage, whereas end-to-end convolutional models generalize across subjects with realistic, uninflated performance. Strict subject-wise validation is strongly recommended as standard practice for translational EEG research.
articles.author: Kalyanaraman Pattabiraman
